subject: Physiology
q: In longstanding hypertension with LV hypertrophy, a low-pitched extra sound is heard just before S1 at the apex. What produces this sound?
opts: Rapid ventricular filling in early diastole striking a dilated ventricle
Opening snap of a stenotic mitral valve
Atrial contraction (atrial kick) into a stiff, noncompliant hypertrophied ventricle
why: This describes the S3 mechanism, not S4.
Mitral closure produces S1, not this pre-S1 sound.
An opening snap occurs after S2 in mitral stenosis, not just before S1.
Correct - S4 is produced by atrial contraction forcing blood into a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle.
exp: S4 is a late-diastolic sound from atrial contraction into a stiff, noncompliant ventricle (hypertension, aortic stenosis, HCM); it is absent in atrial fibrillation as it needs coordinated atrial contraction.

subject: Physiology
q: In heart failure with atrial stretch from volume overload, a cardiac hormone promotes natriuresis/diuresis by inhibiting collecting-duct sodium reabsorption and suppressing renin. Identify it.
why: Correct - ANP is released from stretched atrial myocytes and promotes natriuresis while suppressing renin/aldosterone.
Aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption, the opposite effect.
ADH promotes water reabsorption via aquaporin-2, not primarily natriuresis.
Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor stimulating sodium retention.
exp: ANP, released from atrial myocytes in response to wall stretch, promotes natriuresis/diuresis, dilates the afferent arteriole to raise GFR, and suppresses renin/aldosterone - a counter-regulatory hormone opposing the RAAS.

subject: Physiology
q: Which factor makes large-diameter, heavily myelinated A-alpha fibres conduct fastest in the Erlanger-Gasser classification?
opts: Larger axon diameter and greater myelination (saltatory conduction)
why: Resting membrane potential is similar across fibre types.
Correct - larger diameter and myelination allow fast saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier.
Extracellular calcium affects transmitter release/threshold, not axonal conduction.
Axon length affects total conduction time, not velocity.
exp: Conduction velocity rises with axon diameter (less internal resistance) and myelination (saltatory conduction) - why A-alpha fibres conduct fastest and unmyelinated C fibres slowest.

subject: Physiology
q: Transection of the brainstem at the mid-pontine level -- between the pneumotaxic centre (upper pons) and the apneustic centre (lower pons) -- with vagi intact, produces prolonged deep inspiratory gasps. Which centre, unopposed, produces this pattern?
why: The dorsal group generates the basic inspiratory rhythm but is not responsible for this specific pattern.
The ventral group is mainly active in forced breathing.
Correct - the apneustic centre drives prolonged inspiration when unopposed by the pneumotaxic centre.
Central chemoreceptors drive ventilatory rate via CSF H+/CO2, unrelated to this lesion.
exp: The apneustic centre in the lower pons drives prolonged inspiratory effort and is normally checked by the pneumotaxic centre (upper pons); removing pneumotaxic input produces unopposed apneustic breathing.

subject: Physiology
q: After a left MCA stroke, a patient speaks in slow, effortful, non-fluent, telegraphic sentences with relatively preserved comprehension. Which area is affected?
why: Wernicke's lesions cause fluent, nonsensical speech with poor comprehension, the opposite pattern.
Angular gyrus lesions cause alexia/agraphia (Gerstmann syndrome).
Primary auditory cortex lesions cause cortical deafness.
Correct - Broca's area damage produces non-fluent, telegraphic speech with relatively preserved comprehension.
exp: Broca's (expressive/motor) aphasia results from damage to the posterior inferior frontal gyrus, producing non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension, contrasted with fluent Wernicke's aphasia.

subject: Physiology
q: A dilated, failing left ventricle needs higher myocardial oxygen demand to generate the same intraventricular pressure as a normal-sized ventricle. Which principle explains this?
opts: Law of Laplace (wall tension proportional to pressure times radius, inversely to wall thickness)
why: Correct - dilatation increases radius, raising wall tension and oxygen demand for the same pressure.
Frank-Starling relates preload to stroke volume, not wall tension.
The Bainbridge reflex is a heart-rate response to atrial stretch.
The Fick principle calculates cardiac output from oxygen consumption.
exp: By the Law of Laplace, wall tension equals pressure times radius divided by twice the wall thickness; ventricular dilatation without compensatory wall thickening raises wall tension and oxygen demand, explaining energetic inefficiency in dilated hearts.

subject: Physiology
q: Which neurotransmitter is released by all preganglionic autonomic neurons, both sympathetic and parasympathetic?
why: Norepinephrine is the postganglionic sympathetic transmitter (except sweat glands), not preganglionic
Correct — all preganglionic fibres release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors
Dopamine is a CNS transmitter, not a standard ganglionic transmitter
Epinephrine is the adrenal medulla's hormonal output, not a preganglionic neurotransmitter
exp: All preganglionic autonomic fibres, sympathetic and parasympathetic alike, release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors on the postganglionic neuron; norepinephrine is a postganglionic sympathetic transmitter, not a preganglionic one.

subject: Physiology
q: Which Korotkoff sound phase is used to define diastolic blood pressure during routine cuff auscultation?
why: Phase I is the systolic marker, not diastolic
Phase II is a mid-sequence murmur/swishing quality, not the diastolic marker
Phase IV muffling is used for diastolic only when sounds don't disappear, e.g. pregnancy or severe AR
Correct — disappearance of sound (Phase V) is the standard diastolic BP marker
exp: Phase I marks systolic BP; disappearance of sound (Phase V) is the standard clinical marker for diastolic BP, with Phase IV muffling reserved for situations where sounds persist to zero.

subject: Physiology
q: Which segment of the nephron remains impermeable to water even in the presence of maximal ADH?
opts: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Descending thin limb of the loop of Henle
why: Correct — TAL lacks aquaporins entirely, always water-impermeable
PCT is highly water-permeable (aquaporin-1), reabsorbing ~65% of filtrate isosmotically
Cortical collecting duct permeability is ADH-dependent via aquaporin-2 insertion, not fixed
Descending thin limb is freely water-permeable, allowing water to leave into the hypertonic interstitium
exp: The thick ascending limb actively pumps NaCl out via NKCC2 but has no aquaporins, so it stays water-impermeable at all times — this is what makes it the diluting segment and generates the hypertonic medullary interstitium, independent of ADH.

subject: Physiology
q: Which part of the tracheobronchial tree offers the greatest total resistance to airflow?
why: Trachea is a single large-diameter conduit with low resistance
Terminal bronchioles' huge combined cross-sectional area makes total resistance here low despite tiny individual lumens
Correct — medium bronchi give the highest total resistance
Alveolar ducts have an even greater cross-sectional area than terminal bronchioles, contributing negligible resistance
exp: Terminal bronchioles have tiny individual lumens but an enormous combined cross-sectional area, so their total resistance is low; medium-sized bronchi combine moderate individual calibre with fewer parallel branches, giving them the highest total airway resistance.

subject: Physiology
q: A 30-year-old woman with three days of profuse watery diarrhoea has an arterial blood gas: pH 7.30, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, PaCO2 24 mmHg. Using Winter's formula, is the respiratory response appropriate for this metabolic acidosis?
opts: No — PaCO2 should be lower for adequate compensation, indicating a superimposed respiratory alkalosis
Yes — the PaCO2 falls within the predicted compensatory range
No — PaCO2 should be higher, indicating a superimposed respiratory acidosis
Compensation cannot be assessed without a simultaneous urine pH
why: PaCO2 would need to fall below the predicted range (under 21) to suggest an added respiratory alkalosis, which isn't the case
Correct — 24 mmHg lies inside the 21-25 mmHg predicted window, so compensation is appropriate
A PaCO2 above 25 would suggest inadequate compensation or superimposed respiratory acidosis, not seen here
Winter's formula uses only HCO3- and PaCO2 from the same ABG; urine pH is not required
exp: Winter's formula predicts expected PaCO2 = (1.5 x HCO3-) + 8 +/- 2; for HCO3- of 10, expected PaCO2 = 23 +/- 2 (21-25 mmHg) — a measured value of 24 falls inside this window, confirming appropriate respiratory compensation for the primary metabolic acidosis from diarrhoea-related bicarbonate loss.

subject: Physiology
q: A 55-year-old man being evaluated for tabes dorsalis is found to have bilateral small, irregular pupils that constrict briskly on convergence for near vision but fail to constrict when a light is shone directly into either eye. What is this pupillary finding called, and which reflex pathway is selectively disrupted?
opts: Argyll Robertson pupil; the light reflex pathway (pretectal nucleus) is disrupted while the near/accommodation reflex pathway is spared
Marcus Gunn pupil; afferent pupillary defect from optic nerve damage
Adie's tonic pupil; postganglionic parasympathetic denervation with light-near dissociation reversed
Horner's syndrome; sympathetic pathway disruption causing miosis
why: Correct — this is the classic Argyll Robertson description, from selective pretectal (light reflex) pathway damage with a spared near-reflex pathway
Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect) is unilateral and tested by the swinging-flashlight test, reflecting optic nerve disease, not bilateral light-near dissociation
Adie's pupil shows a tonically dilated, usually unilateral pupil with a slow sustained near response and poor light response, from ciliary ganglion damage
Horner's syndrome causes miosis with ptosis and anhidrosis from sympathetic loss, not light-near dissociation
exp: Argyll Robertson pupils show light-near dissociation — pupils react to accommodation/convergence but not to light — classically from a midbrain pretectal lesion (neurosyphilis/tabes dorsalis); the near-reflex pathway is anatomically distinct and escapes the lesion.

subject: Physiology
q: Following section of a peripheral motor nerve, the denervated skeletal muscle fibre becomes sensitive to acetylcholine over its entire surface membrane, not just at the original end-plate region. What is this phenomenon called?
why: Describes what happens to the axon distal to a nerve injury, not the muscle membrane receptor change.
A distinct phenomenon of increasing contraction force with repeated stimulation, unrelated to denervation.
Not a standard term; regeneration refers to axonal regrowth, not receptor spread.
Correct — extrajunctional ACh receptors spread across the fibre after denervation.
exp: After denervation, extrajunctional ACh receptors proliferate across the entire muscle fibre membrane (not just the neuromuscular junction), making the fibre abnormally sensitive to circulating or locally applied acetylcholine - this denervation hypersensitivity underlies the spontaneous fibrillation potentials seen on EMG in denervated muscle, a key clue to lower motor neuron lesions.

subject: Physiology
q: Which laboratory test assesses red blood cell resistance to lysis when exposed to graded hypotonic saline solutions, and is characteristically increased (cells lyse at higher, less-dilute concentrations) in hereditary spherocytosis?
why: Correct — spherocytes lyse at higher (less dilute) saline concentrations due to reduced surface-area-to-volume ratio.
Detects antibody-mediated hemolysis (autoimmune hemolytic anemia), not membrane-shape-related fragility.
Screens for HbS-related sickling under hypoxia, unrelated to osmotic fragility.
Reflects marrow response to hemolysis/anemia generally, not a specific fragility measurement.
exp: The osmotic fragility test exposes RBCs to progressively hypotonic saline; because spherocytes have a reduced surface-area-to-volume ratio, they are less able to swell before lysing, so they hemolyse at a higher (less dilute) saline concentration than normal biconcave RBCs - this increased osmotic fragility is a hallmark diagnostic finding in hereditary spherocytosis.

subject: Physiology
q: When a person steps on a sharp object, the stimulated limb reflexively flexes and withdraws while the opposite limb extends to bear the added weight. What are these two linked spinal reflexes called?
opts: Stretch reflex and Golgi tendon reflex
Flexor (withdrawal) reflex and crossed extensor reflex
why: Monosynaptic/autogenic inhibitory reflexes, not the withdrawal-plus-postural-support pair described.
Correct — a polysynaptic protective reflex paired with contralateral postural support.
A cortical/pyramidal tract sign tested by plantar stimulation, unrelated to this protective withdrawal mechanism.
Underlying circuit mechanisms that modulate reflexes generally, but not the named reflex pair itself.
exp: The flexor withdrawal reflex is a polysynaptic, protective spinal reflex that removes a limb from a noxious stimulus; because this shifts body weight, an accompanying crossed extensor reflex extends the contralateral limb through commissural interneurons to maintain postural support - together illustrating integrated polysynaptic spinal reflex circuitry distinct from the simple monosynaptic stretch reflex.

subject: Physiology
q: Which pulmonary function test measures the lung's capacity to transfer a gas across the alveolar-capillary membrane, and is reduced in both emphysema (loss of surface area) and pulmonary fibrosis (thickened membrane)?
why: Reflects large airway function/effort, used mainly in asthma monitoring, not diffusion capacity.
Distinguishes obstructive from restrictive patterns but doesn't directly measure gas transfer across the membrane.
Correct — reduced in both emphysema and fibrosis, for different reasons.
A lung volume measurement, not a diffusion measure.
exp: DLCO measures how efficiently carbon monoxide diffuses from alveolar gas into pulmonary capillary blood, reflecting the functional surface area and thickness of the alveolar-capillary membrane; it is reduced in emphysema (destroyed alveolar surface area) and interstitial fibrosis (thickened diffusion membrane), even though these diseases show opposite spirometric patterns, making DLCO useful to distinguish causes of dyspnea beyond spirometry alone.

subject: Physiology
q: Aldosterone acts on which renal tubular segment to increase sodium reabsorption via epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), while promoting potassium and hydrogen ion secretion?
opts: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Descending limb of the loop of Henle
Principal cells of the cortical collecting duct
why: Reabsorbs about 65-70% of filtered sodium/bicarbonate largely independent of aldosterone regulation.
Site of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (loop diuretic target), not the main aldosterone action site.
Primarily water-permeable, not the site of aldosterone-mediated sodium transport.
Correct — aldosterone upregulates ENaC here, driving K+ and H+ secretion.
exp: Aldosterone, released from the zona glomerulosa in response to angiotensin II or hyperkalemia, acts on principal cells of the cortical collecting duct (and late distal tubule) to upregulate ENaC-mediated sodium reabsorption and, via the electrochemical gradient created, drives potassium secretion through ROMK channels and hydrogen ion secretion by adjacent intercalated cells - the basis of both its volume/potassium homeostasis role and Conn's syndrome (hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis).

subject: Physiology
q: After a peripheral nerve is transected, the axon segment distal to the site of injury undergoes degeneration along with its myelin sheath, while the proximal stump may begin to regenerate. What is this distal degenerative process called?
why: Correct — anterograde breakdown of the distal axon and myelin after transection.
Refers to changes in the neuronal cell body (Nissl substance dispersion) after axonal injury, not the distal axon/myelin breakdown itself.
A muscle membrane receptor change following denervation, not the axonal degeneration process itself.
A distant, functional depression of neural activity following a remote CNS lesion (e.g., stroke), an unrelated concept.
exp: Wallerian degeneration describes the anterograde breakdown of the axon and myelin distal to a nerve transection, since the distal segment is cut off from the cell body's protein synthesis machinery; Schwann cells then proliferate and, with macrophages, clear debris to form bands of Buengner that guide regenerating axon sprouts from the proximal stump - the physiological basis for peripheral nerve repair surgery timelines.

subject: Physiology
q: Stiffening of skeletal muscle after death, from persistent actin-myosin cross-bridge formation, occurs primarily due to depletion of which molecule?
why: Calcium initiates cross-bridge cycling, but its persistence alone doesn't explain the fixed rigor state
Troponin C permits cross-bridge formation but isn't the depleted molecule
Correct
Acetylcholine triggers the initial NMJ action potential, not cross-bridge detachment
exp: Rigor mortis occurs because postmortem ATP depletion prevents myosin heads from detaching from actin (ATP is required to break, not form, the cross-bridge), fixing muscle in a contracted state until autolytic proteolysis resolves it.

subject: Physiology
q: Nitric oxide and atrial natriuretic peptide produce vascular smooth muscle relaxation predominantly through which second-messenger pathway?
why: cAMP-PKA mediates beta-adrenergic effects, not NO/ANP relaxation
IP3-DAG (Gq) mediates alpha-1 vasoconstriction, the opposite effect
Correct
NO/ANP act via enzymatic messengers, not direct ligand-gated channels
exp: NO activates soluble guanylyl cyclase and ANP activates particulate guanylyl cyclase, both raising intracellular cGMP, which activates PKG to lower intracellular calcium and dephosphorylate myosin light chain, relaxing smooth muscle - the basis of nitrate and sildenafil pharmacology.

subject: Physiology
q: A patient speaks fluently with normal grammar but meaningless content, and comprehension of spoken language is severely impaired. This localizes a lesion to which area?
why: Broca's lesions cause non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension
Correct
Arcuate fasciculus lesions cause conduction aphasia - fluent speech, intact comprehension, impaired repetition
Primary motor cortex lesions cause weakness, not language deficits
exp: Wernicke's aphasia (receptive/fluent) results from a posterior superior temporal gyrus lesion (usually left, inferior division MCA), producing fluent but nonsensical speech with impaired comprehension - opposite to Broca's non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension.

subject: Physiology
q: Deoxygenated hemoglobin has a higher affinity for carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions than oxygenated hemoglobin, facilitating CO2 loading in peripheral tissues. This is termed which effect?
why: Bohr effect describes the reverse - CO2/pH shifting hemoglobin's oxygen affinity
Correct
Bainbridge reflex increases heart rate with atrial stretch, unrelated to gas transport
Root effect is a fish-specific phenomenon, not seen in mammals
exp: The Haldane effect describes how deoxygenation of hemoglobin in peripheral capillaries increases its capacity to carry CO2 and H+, promoting CO2 uptake in tissues and release in the lungs on reoxygenation - complementary to but distinct from the Bohr effect.

subject: Physiology
q: If GFR is 125 mL/min and renal plasma flow is 625 mL/min, what is the filtration fraction?
why: Would require an RPF of 1250 mL/min, not given
Underestimates the given ratio
Correct
Would require an RPF of 500 mL/min, not given
exp: Filtration fraction equals GFR/RPF, so 125/625 = 0.20 or 20%; normally about one-fifth of plasma flowing through the glomerulus is filtered, rising with efferent arteriolar constriction and falling with afferent constriction.

subject: Physiology
q: In hypocalcemia, carpal spasm appears on cuff inflation above systolic pressure (Trousseau's sign). Low ionic calcium causes neuromuscular excitability by which mechanism?
opts: Increased acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
Decreased threshold for opening of voltage-gated sodium channels
why: Hypocalcemia reduces, not increases, presynaptic ACh release - not the tetany mechanism
Correct
Tetany is due to sodium channel threshold change, not potassium conductance
Low calcium reduces troponin C binding, impairing rather than increasing contraction
exp: Extracellular calcium normally stabilizes voltage-gated sodium channels near the pore; hypocalcemia lowers the threshold at which these channels open, so smaller depolarizations trigger action potentials, producing the spontaneous firing behind hypocalcemic tetany.

subject: Physiology
q: The cardiac sodium-calcium exchanger (NCX) extrudes one calcium ion in exchange for the entry of three sodium ions, using the sodium gradient. This is an example of which transport mechanism?
why: Primary active transport directly uses ATP hydrolysis; NCX uses the sodium gradient instead
Facilitated diffusion moves a solute down its own gradient without coupling
Simple diffusion needs no carrier protein
Correct
exp: NCX uses the electrochemical sodium gradient (established by primary active Na-K ATPase) to drive calcium extrusion against its gradient - a secondary active, antiport mechanism, distinct from symport carriers like SGLT1 that move solutes in the same direction as sodium.

subject: Physiology
q: At the sarcomere length producing maximum isometric tetanic tension in skeletal muscle, actin and myosin filaments show which degree of overlap?
opts: Complete overlap, with actin filaments overlapping each other in the centre of the sarcomere
Optimal overlap allowing the maximum number of myosin cross-bridges to engage thin filaments without steric hindrance
No overlap between thick and thin filaments
Overlap only at the extreme ends of the thick filament, abutting the Z-line
why: Over-shortened sarcomere - actin filaments interfere with each other, tension falls
Correct - optimal cross-bridge number at resting sarcomere length (~2.0-2.2 micrometers)
Over-stretched - zero cross-bridges, zero tension
Describes an over-stretched state with minimal tension, not maximum
exp: The length-tension relationship of skeletal muscle peaks at the resting sarcomere length where the maximum number of myosin heads can form cross-bridges with actin without steric interference - shortening or overstretching beyond this reduces active tension generated.

subject: Physiology
q: Which indicator-dilution technique is used to estimate plasma volume in humans?
why: Correct - dye-albumin complex stays confined to the vascular compartment
Inulin marks ECF volume, not plasma volume specifically
Deuterium oxide marks total body water
Antipyrine also marks total body water, freely diffusible
exp: Plasma volume is measured using dyes or labelled proteins confined to the vascular compartment such as Evans blue bound to albumin, while inulin marks ECF volume and deuterium oxide or antipyrine mark total body water - know which indicator maps to which fluid compartment.

subject: Physiology
q: Which EEG wave pattern is characteristically seen during REM sleep, resembling the pattern of an awake, alert individual?
opts: Low-amplitude, high-frequency beta or desynchronized activity
why: Delta waves mark stage N3 deep slow-wave sleep, not REM
Spindles and K-complexes mark stage N2
Correct - REM is called paradoxical sleep due to this desynchronized fast pattern
Alpha waves mark relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed
exp: REM sleep is called paradoxical sleep because the EEG shows low-amplitude, high-frequency desynchronized activity resembling wakefulness, despite the person being asleep with atonic skeletal muscle - a key point distinguishing REM from the slow delta waves of deep NREM sleep.

subject: Physiology
q: An increase in 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) within red blood cells shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve in which direction, and with what functional effect?
opts: Left shift, increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen
No shift - 2,3-DPG only affects fetal hemoglobin
Left shift, decreasing oxygen unloading at tissues
Right shift, decreasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen and facilitating oxygen release to tissues
why: Wrong direction, describes low 2,3-DPG states like fetal hemoglobin
2,3-DPG affects adult hemoglobin far more than fetal hemoglobin
Wrong direction, would reduce rather than increase unloading
Correct - stabilizes the low-affinity T-state, aiding tissue oxygen delivery
exp: 2,3-DPG binds preferentially to deoxyhemoglobin's beta chains, stabilizing the low-affinity T-state - its rise with high altitude, chronic anemia, or chronic hypoxemia shifts the curve right, aiding tissue oxygen delivery, while stored blood loses 2,3-DPG over time which can transiently impair oxygen unloading after massive transfusion.

subject: Physiology
q: Approximately what fraction of filtered bicarbonate is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule via the Na+/H+ antiporter-carbonic anhydrase mechanism?
opts: 100%, entirely in the proximal convoluted tubule
40-50%, equally split between proximal tubule and loop of Henle
why: Correct - proximal tubule reabsorbs roughly two-thirds of filtered bicarbonate
Remainder is reclaimed in the thick ascending limb and distal intercalated cells
Underestimates proximal tubule contribution and misattributes bulk to distal tubule
Incorrect proportion
exp: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about 65-70% of filtered bicarbonate using the apical Na+/H+ exchanger NHE3 and carbonic anhydrase - carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide act here, producing a mild proximal type 2 RTA-like bicarbonate wasting.

subject: Physiology
q: Muscle fatigue during sustained high-intensity exercise is most closely correlated with intracellular accumulation of which substance, alongside phosphocreatine depletion?
opts: Hydrogen ions from lactic acidosis and inorganic phosphate
Calcium ions accumulating in the sarcoplasmic reticulum
why: Acetylcholine accumulation is not the mechanism of peripheral muscle fatigue
Correct - anaerobic glycolysis produces lactate and H+, and inorganic phosphate accumulates from ATP and phosphocreatine breakdown
Sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release is actually impaired during fatigue, not accumulated
Myoglobin is an oxygen-storage protein unrelated to the fatigue mechanism
exp: Peripheral muscle fatigue during intense exercise is driven mainly by accumulation of inorganic phosphate and hydrogen ions from anaerobic glycolysis, which impair cross-bridge cycling and calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum - central fatigue is a separate additional mechanism.

subject: Physiology
q: Which buffer system is the predominant intracellular buffer, in contrast to bicarbonate being the dominant extracellular buffer?
why: Bicarbonate is the principal extracellular buffer, not intracellular
Ammonia buffering occurs in renal tubular fluid for hydrogen ion excretion, not as a general intracellular buffer
Correct - phosphate and proteins including hemoglobin are the major intracellular buffers
Citrate is not a physiological body buffer of note
exp: While bicarbonate dominates extracellular buffering because it is an open system linked to respiratory carbon dioxide excretion, the intracellular compartment relies chiefly on phosphate and protein buffers including hemoglobin, which buffers hydrogen ions generated from carbon dioxide in red cells.

subject: Physiology
q: During excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle, depolarization sensed by the dihydropyridine (DHP) receptor on the T-tubule directly triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via which receptor?
opts: Voltage-gated L-type calcium channel on the SR membrane
why: IP3 receptors mediate calcium release in smooth muscle/non-excitable cells, not this mechanism
Not a distinct SR channel in this pathway; the DHP receptor itself is the T-tubule sensor
Mediates neuromuscular transmission at the motor end plate, not SR calcium release
Correct
exp: In skeletal muscle the DHP receptor is mechanically coupled to the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on the SR; depolarization causes a conformational change that directly opens RyR1 releasing calcium, unlike cardiac muscle which relies on calcium-induced calcium release.

subject: Physiology
q: The fluid mosaic model describing the cell membrane, with globular proteins floating within a fluid lipid bilayer, was proposed by:
why: Proposed the earlier protein-lipid-protein sandwich model
First demonstrated the lipid bilayer arrangement, not the mosaic protein arrangement
Correct
Proposed the lipid-solubility theory of membrane permeability
exp: Singer and Nicolson (1972) proposed the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane, superseding the earlier Danielli-Davson sandwich model and Gorter-Grendel's bilayer concept.

subject: Physiology
q: The principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, acting via chloride-channel-linked receptors to hyperpolarize neurons, is:
why: Correct
Principal inhibitory transmitter of the spinal cord, not the brain
The principal excitatory neurotransmitter of the CNS
A monoamine involved in reward/motor pathways, not the principal inhibitory transmitter
exp: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain (acting on GABA-A chloride channels and GABA-B receptors), while glycine plays the equivalent inhibitory role predominantly in the spinal cord.

subject: Physiology
q: Static lung compliance (change in volume per unit change in pressure) is characteristically increased in which of the following conditions?
why: Reduces compliance (stiff, fibrotic lung)
Correct
Reduces compliance (diffuse alveolar damage, stiff lung)
Reduces compliance locally due to consolidation
exp: Emphysema destroys alveolar septa and elastic tissue, reducing elastic recoil and increasing compliance (lungs distend easily but recoil poorly); fibrosis, ARDS, and pneumonia are restrictive/stiffening processes that reduce compliance.

subject: Physiology
q: The counter-current multiplier mechanism that generates a hypertonic medullary interstitium, enabling the kidney to concentrate urine, is located in the:
why: Site of bulk isosmotic reabsorption, not gradient generation
Fine-tunes electrolyte reabsorption, not the multiplier
Uses the gradient (with vasa recta as counter-current exchanger) rather than generating it
Correct
exp: The loop of Henle, with differential permeability of its thin descending and thick ascending limbs, acts as the counter-current multiplier building the medullary osmotic gradient; the collecting duct then uses this gradient plus ADH-regulated water permeability to concentrate urine.

subject: Physiology
q: Miniature end-plate potentials (MEPPs), recorded at the neuromuscular junction even without nerve stimulation, result from the spontaneous release of:
opts: Acetylcholine released continuously from the axon membrane
Calcium influx alone, without any acetylcholine release
A single quantum (one vesicle) of acetylcholine
why: ACh release is quantal/vesicular, not a continuous membrane process
Calcium influx triggers vesicle fusion but is not itself the released substance producing the potential
Correct
This enzyme degrades ACh, it does not generate a potential
exp: MEPPs are small spontaneous depolarizations produced by random release of single acetylcholine-containing vesicles (quanta) from the presynaptic terminal; a nerve action potential normally releases many quanta simultaneously to produce a full end-plate potential.

subject: Physiology
q: Antidiuretic hormone increases water permeability of the renal collecting duct principal cells by which cellular mechanism?
opts: V2 receptor-mediated insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane
Parathyroid hormone-mediated distal tubular calcium reabsorption
why: This correctly describes the mechanism of ADH action
This describes aldosterone's sodium-reabsorption mechanism, a separate hormonal pathway
ANP promotes natriuresis and diuresis, opposite to ADH's antidiuretic action
PTH acts on the distal tubule for calcium, unrelated to ADH's water-permeability effect
exp: ADH binds basolateral V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells, activating a Gs-cAMP-PKA cascade that triggers insertion of pre-formed aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane - this is the molecular basis for the concentrating defect in diabetes insipidus.

subject: Physiology
q: Which subunit of the troponin complex binds tropomyosin and helps anchor the complex along the actin filament?
why: Troponin C is the calcium-binding subunit, not the tropomyosin-binding one
Troponin I inhibits the actin-myosin interaction at rest, a different function
Calmodulin is a distinct calcium-binding regulatory protein, not a troponin subunit, and plays no role in anchoring the complex to actin
This correctly identifies Troponin T as the tropomyosin-binding subunit
exp: The troponin complex has three subunits with distinct roles: Troponin C binds calcium, Troponin I inhibits actin-myosin interaction at rest, and Troponin T binds tropomyosin, anchoring the complex onto the thin filament - Troponin T is also the cardiac biomarker used clinically for myocardial injury.

subject: Physiology
q: Activation of a Gs protein-coupled receptor leads to which downstream second-messenger cascade?
opts: Gq protein leading to phospholipase C and the IP3/DAG pathway
Gi protein leading to decreased adenylate cyclase activity and decreased cAMP
Gs protein leading to increased adenylate cyclase activity, increased cAMP, and PKA activation
Direct opening of a ligand-gated ion channel
why: This describes Gq-coupled receptor signaling, a separate pathway from Gs
This describes Gi-coupled receptor signaling, the functional opposite of Gs
This correctly describes the Gs pathway
This describes ionotropic receptor signaling, unrelated to G-protein coupling
exp: Gs-coupled receptors (e.g. beta-adrenergic receptors) stimulate adenylate cyclase, raising intracellular cAMP, which activates protein kinase A to phosphorylate downstream targets - the opposite of Gi-coupled receptors, which inhibit adenylate cyclase.

subject: Physiology
q: Pulmonary surfactant, produced by type II pneumocytes, reduces alveolar surface tension mainly through which phospholipid component?
why: Sphingomyelin is used as the reference compound in the lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio test, not the active surface-tension-reducing agent
This correctly identifies DPPC as the principal functional component of surfactant
Phosphatidylserine is a minor membrane phospholipid, not the primary surfactant component
Cholesterol is a minor surfactant component that modulates fluidity, not the principal surface-tension reducer
exp: DPPC is the principal surface-tension-lowering component of pulmonary surfactant, packing tightly at the air-liquid interface to prevent alveolar collapse at low lung volumes - its deficiency in preterm infants underlies neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

subject: Physiology
q: Cardiac output can be calculated using the Fick principle from oxygen consumption and which two other measured values?
opts: Arterial and mixed venous oxygen content difference
Heart rate and stroke volume measured directly
Central venous pressure and mean arterial pressure
why: This correctly identifies the Fick equation's required inputs alongside oxygen consumption
This is the basic cardiac output formula, but doesn't describe the Fick method, which avoids needing a direct stroke volume measurement
Blood pressure values are used for other hemodynamic calculations, not the Fick method
CVP and MAP are used to estimate perfusion pressure, not cardiac output via Fick
exp: The Fick principle calculates cardiac output as oxygen consumption divided by the arteriovenous oxygen content difference - used clinically during cardiac catheterization when direct measurement of stroke volume is not feasible.

subject: Physiology
q: Glucose appears in the urine once plasma glucose exceeds the renal threshold, corresponding to saturation of SGLT2 transporters at approximately what plasma glucose level?
why: This is below the normal fasting range and far below the actual threshold
This is close to but below the accepted renal threshold value
This overstates the threshold beyond the standard teaching value
This correctly identifies approximately 180 mg/dL as the classically taught renal threshold for glucose
exp: The renal threshold for glucose is approximately 180 mg/dL, above which the SGLT2 transporters in the proximal convoluted tubule become saturated and cannot reabsorb all filtered glucose, resulting in glucosuria - the physiological rationale behind SGLT2 inhibitor drugs.

subject: Physiology
q: A comatose patient extends both arms and legs rigidly with wrist pronation on a painful stimulus. This decerebrate posturing localizes the lesion to which level, and how does it differ from decorticate posturing?
opts: At or below the red nucleus (midbrain-pons); decorticate shows arm flexion with leg extension, a rostrally-located lesion
Above the red nucleus (cortex/subcortex); decorticate shows arm extension
At the level of the spinal cord only; decorticate is identical
In the cerebellum exclusively; decorticate involves no leg response
why: Correct - decerebrate posturing indicates a lesion at or below the red nucleus, releasing extensor tone; decorticate posturing indicates a more rostral lesion above the red nucleus.
Reverses the localization logic.
A purely spinal lesion would not produce this stereotyped brainstem-mediated posturing.
Cerebellar lesions do not classically produce either posture.
exp: Decerebrate (all-limb extension) posturing localizes at or below the red nucleus, while decorticate (arm flexion, leg extension) localizes above it - a bedside localizing sign every ward doctor should be able to interpret instantly in a comatose patient.

subject: Physiology
q: In a patient with cardiac tamponade, systolic blood pressure falls by more than 10 mmHg during normal inspiration. What is this sign called, and what is its mechanism?
opts: Kussmaul sign; increased jugular venous pressure on inspiration
Pulsus paradoxus; exaggerated inspiratory fall in left ventricular stroke volume due to increased right ventricular filling within a fixed pericardial space
Pulsus alternans; alternating strong and weak beats due to systolic dysfunction
Pulsus bisferiens; two systolic peaks due to aortic regurgitation
why: Kussmaul sign is a paradoxical rise in JVP with inspiration, a different sign seen in constrictive pericarditis.
Correct - the fixed pericardial space forces septal bulging into the LV during inspiratory RV filling, exaggerating the normal inspiratory fall in stroke volume.
Pulsus alternans reflects alternating contractile strength in severe LV dysfunction, unrelated to respiration.
Pulsus bisferiens is a double-peaked pulse seen in aortic regurgitation/HOCM.
exp: Pulsus paradoxus greater than 10 mmHg is a key bedside sign of cardiac tamponade physiology, caused by exaggerated ventricular interdependence within the non-compliant, fluid-filled pericardial sac - it also occurs (via a different mechanism) in severe asthma/COPD.

subject: Physiology
q: A patient with renal artery stenosis has reduced renal perfusion pressure. Which juxtaglomerular apparatus mechanism is primarily responsible for the resulting rise in plasma renin?
opts: Macula densa cells sense increased NaCl delivery to the distal tubule and suppress renin
Efferent arteriolar dilation directly triggers renin release
Reduced afferent arteriolar wall stretch (baroreceptor mechanism) and reduced NaCl delivery to the macula densa both stimulate renin release from granular cells
Increased GFR directly stimulates renin secretion
why: Reverses the macula densa relationship - reduced, not increased, NaCl delivery stimulates renin.
It is afferent, not efferent, arteriolar tone that drives the baroreceptor mechanism.
Correct - both the intrarenal baroreceptor mechanism (granular cells) and reduced macula densa NaCl sensing converge to stimulate renin release.
Increased GFR would reduce, not stimulate, renin release via the macula densa pathway.
exp: Renin release is controlled by two coupled JGA sensors - granular cell stretch (afferent arteriolar pressure) and macula densa NaCl delivery - both of which are activated by reduced renal perfusion, as in renal artery stenosis, to drive RAAS activation.

subject: Physiology
q: In an upright healthy adult, ventilation-perfusion ratio differs between the lung apex and base. Which statement correctly describes this and its consequence?
opts: V/Q is higher at the base than the apex, making the base relatively more ventilated than perfused
V/Q is uniform throughout the lung in the upright position
V/Q is highest at the base because perfusion is lowest there
V/Q is higher at the apex than the base, because perfusion falls faster than ventilation going up the lung due to gravity
why: Reverses the correct relationship.
V/Q is markedly non-uniform in the upright lung.
Perfusion is actually highest, not lowest, at the base.
Correct - perfusion falls more steeply than ventilation from base to apex under gravity, giving the apex a higher V/Q.
exp: The apex is relatively over-ventilated relative to blood flow (high V/Q, dead-space-like) while the base is relatively over-perfused relative to ventilation (low V/Q, shunt-like) - this gradient underlies why apical TB and basal aspiration pneumonia behave differently physiologically.

subject: Physiology
q: Plasma proteins carry a net negative charge and cannot cross the capillary membrane freely. According to the Gibbs-Donnan effect, how does this influence distribution of diffusible ions across the capillary wall?
opts: It causes a slightly higher concentration of diffusible cations (e.g., Na+) and a slightly lower concentration of diffusible anions (e.g., Cl-) on the protein-containing side, to maintain electroneutrality
It has no effect on ion distribution since proteins are too large to matter
It equally distributes all ions regardless of charge
It causes complete exclusion of all cations from the protein-containing compartment
why: Correct - to preserve electroneutrality, diffusible cations are drawn slightly higher and diffusible anions slightly lower on the protein-containing side.
Understates a real, measurable effect on the plasma-interstitial ion gradient.
Contradicts the charge-based redistribution that defines the phenomenon.
Overstates the effect - cations are enriched, not excluded.
exp: The Gibbs-Donnan effect is a small but real contributor to the difference in ion concentration (and effective osmotic pressure) between plasma and interstitial fluid, driven purely by the non-diffusible negative charge on plasma proteins.

subject: Physiology
q: A patient develops loss of pain and temperature sensation over both shoulders and upper arms in a cape-like distribution, with preserved fine touch and proprioception in the same area. Which lesion and mechanism best explain this dissociated sensory loss?
opts: Dorsal column lesion; loss of touch/proprioception with sparing of pain/temperature
Syringomyelia damaging decussating spinothalamic fibers at the ventral white commissure, sparing the dorsal columns
Complete spinal cord transection at the cervical level
Peripheral neuropathy affecting only large myelinated fibers
why: Describes the opposite sensory pattern to this case.
Correct - a central cervical cavity first damages the crossing spinothalamic fibers at the ventral white commissure, sparing the more peripheral dorsal columns.
Complete transection would cause loss of all modalities and motor function below the level, not a dissociated pattern.
Peripheral neuropathy of large fibers would impair touch/proprioception, the opposite pattern to this case.
exp: Syringomyelia's classic cape-like (suspended) dissociated sensory loss - pain/temperature lost, touch/proprioception spared - reflects the central expansion of the cavity first interrupting the decussating spinothalamic fibers before it reaches the peripherally-located dorsal columns.

subject: Physiology
q: A young man, after standing for a prolonged period in a hot, crowded room, becomes pale and briefly loses consciousness, with bradycardia and hypotension noted just before the episode. Which reflex mechanism best explains this vasovagal syncope?
opts: Baroreceptor reflex causing appropriate tachycardia and vasoconstriction
Cushing reflex from raised intracranial pressure
Bezold-Jarisch reflex - paradoxical vagal-mediated bradycardia and vasodilation
Bainbridge reflex causing reflex tachycardia from atrial stretch
why: Describes the normal, appropriate baroreceptor response, not what happens in vasovagal syncope.
Cushing reflex responds to raised ICP with hypertension and bradycardia, unrelated to this scenario.
Correct - vigorous contraction of an underfilled ventricle triggers a Bezold-Jarisch-type vagal surge causing paradoxical bradycardia and vasodilation.
Bainbridge reflex causes tachycardia from atrial stretch/volume overload, the opposite direction of change here.
exp: Vasovagal syncope is a paradoxical parasympathetic surge (Bezold-Jarisch-type reflex) triggered by vigorous contraction of an underfilled ventricle, overriding the expected compensatory sympathetic response to reduced venous return - useful to explain to patients as a benign, self-limited reflex rather than a cardiac emergency.

subject: Physiology
q: Spirometry shows FEV1 reduced to 55% of predicted, FVC reduced to 85% of predicted, with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55. Which pattern does this represent?
opts: Restrictive pattern, as in pulmonary fibrosis
Mixed pattern that cannot be determined from these values
Obstructive pattern, as in bronchial asthma/COPD
why: Restrictive disease would show a preserved/high FEV1/FVC ratio, not a reduced one.
Both FEV1 and the ratio are clearly abnormal here.
The pattern is unambiguously obstructive from the reduced ratio alone.
Correct - a disproportionately reduced FEV1 relative to FVC, giving a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio, defines an obstructive pattern.
exp: A reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (here 0.55, well below the normal ~0.75-0.80) with a relatively preserved FVC is the spirometric signature of obstructive lung disease, in contrast to restrictive disease where both values fall proportionately and the ratio is preserved or increased.

subject: Physiology
q: Erythropoietin, the principal stimulus for red cell production, is physiologically secreted mainly by which renal cell type in response to hypoxia?
opts: Peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells of the renal cortex
Principal cells of the collecting duct
why: Juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin in response to reduced renal perfusion pressure, not EPO.
Correct — peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells of the renal cortex and outer medulla are the primary renal EPO source.
Mesangial cells provide structural/contractile support to the glomerular capillary tuft and clear immune complexes, not EPO secretion.
Principal cells of the collecting duct mediate water and sodium reabsorption under ADH/aldosterone control, unrelated to EPO.
exp: Renal EPO is produced chiefly by peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells in the renal cortex and outer medulla, which sense local tissue hypoxia and upregulate EPO transcription via HIF pathways — destruction of these cells in chronic kidney disease is the basis of anemia of CKD.

subject: Physiology
q: On train-of-four nerve stimulation, a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent (e.g., vecuronium) characteristically produces which pattern of response?
opts: Sustained twitch response with no fade
Progressive fade in twitch height across the four stimuli
Post-tetanic potentiation only, with no fade
Initial fasciculation followed by flaccid paralysis with no fade
why: A sustained response without fade is not seen with competitive antagonists at the NMJ.
Correct — progressive TOF fade is the hallmark of non-depolarizing (competitive) block.
Post-tetanic potentiation can follow non-depolarizing block, but the defining TOF finding is the fade itself, not potentiation alone.
Fasciculation followed by flaccid paralysis without fade describes depolarizing (phase I) block from succinylcholine, not a non-depolarizing agent.
exp: Non-depolarizing agents competitively block postsynaptic nicotinic receptors, producing progressive fade on train-of-four and tetanic stimulation because presynaptic receptor blockade impairs the positive-feedback mobilization of acetylcholine needed to sustain repetitive release — the opposite of the sustained, non-fading block from depolarizing agents like succinylcholine.

subject: Physiology
q: Activation of a Gq-protein-coupled receptor stimulates phospholipase C, generating IP3 and DAG. IP3 acts primarily by which mechanism?
opts: Releasing calcium from the endoplasmic/sarcoplasmic reticulum
Activating adenylyl cyclase to raise intracellular cAMP
Opening voltage-gated calcium channels in the plasma membrane
why: Correct — IP3's defining action is binding IP3 receptors on the ER/SR to release stored calcium.
Adenylyl cyclase activation is the Gs-pathway action raising cAMP, a separate second-messenger cascade.
Protein kinase C is activated by DAG (with calcium), not directly by IP3.
Voltage-gated calcium channels open with membrane depolarization, a distinct mechanism from IP3-receptor-mediated ER release.
exp: IP3 diffuses into the cytosol and binds IP3 receptors on the endoplasmic/sarcoplasmic reticulum, opening ligand-gated calcium channels that release stored calcium into the cytoplasm — complementary to DAG, which stays membrane-bound and activates protein kinase C. Keep the Gq (IP3-DAG-calcium) and Gs (cAMP) pathways clearly separated when revising second messengers.

subject: Physiology
q: Alveolar hypoxia causes local pulmonary vasoconstriction, the opposite of the systemic circulation's response to hypoxia, diverting blood flow away from poorly ventilated alveoli toward better-ventilated ones. This is known as?
why: The Bohr effect describes CO2/H+-driven rightward shift of the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve, a gas-transport phenomenon, not a vascular reflex.
Correct — the Euler-Liljestrand mechanism (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction) matches perfusion to ventilation.
The Haldane effect describes how oxygenated hemoglobin carries less CO2, facilitating CO2 unloading at the lungs.
The Bainbridge reflex is atrial-stretch-triggered tachycardia, a cardiac reflex unrelated to pulmonary vascular tone.
exp: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (the Euler-Liljestrand mechanism) redirects pulmonary blood flow away from poorly ventilated alveolar units toward better-ventilated ones, optimizing ventilation-perfusion matching; when generalized (high altitude, COPD), it raises pulmonary vascular resistance and can precipitate cor pulmonale.

subject: Physiology
q: Widened pulse pressure (large difference between systolic and diastolic blood pressure) is characteristically seen in which condition, due to a large stroke volume and rapid diastolic runoff?
why: Aortic stenosis classically produces a narrow pulse pressure with a slow-rising (pulsus parvus et tardus) pulse, the opposite pattern.
Mitral stenosis reduces LV filling and stroke volume, typically giving a normal or narrow pulse pressure.
Correct — aortic regurgitation is the classic cause of a widened pulse pressure with a bounding water-hammer pulse.
Constrictive pericarditis impairs ventricular filling and tends to narrow pulse pressure, with pulsus paradoxus a feature of related tamponade.
exp: In aortic regurgitation, a large total stroke volume (forward plus regurgitant flow) raises systolic pressure, while rapid diastolic backflow into the left ventricle drops diastolic pressure — together widening pulse pressure and producing the bounding water-hammer (Corrigan) pulse and other peripheral signs of AR.

subject: Physiology
q: Creatinine clearance is commonly used clinically to estimate GFR but tends to slightly overestimate true GFR. This is because creatinine, beyond glomerular filtration, also undergoes which additional renal process?
opts: Metabolism within the loop of Henle
Extensive protein binding that reduces filtration
Active secretion by the proximal tubule
why: Creatinine is not meaningfully reabsorbed by the tubules — reabsorption would cause underestimation, not overestimation, of GFR.
Creatinine is not metabolized within the nephron.
Creatinine is not significantly protein-bound, which is precisely why it is freely filtered and useful as a filtration marker.
Correct — a small amount of active tubular secretion adds extra creatinine to urine, causing creatinine clearance to overestimate true GFR.
exp: Creatinine is freely filtered at the glomerulus but also undergoes a small amount of active secretion by proximal tubular organic cation transporters, adding extra creatinine to the urine beyond what was filtered — so creatinine clearance modestly overestimates true GFR, an effect that becomes more pronounced as renal function declines.

subject: Physiology
q: In skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling, calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to which regulatory protein to initiate cross-bridge cycling?
why: Troponin I inhibits actin-myosin interaction at rest but does not itself bind the triggering calcium.
Troponin T anchors the troponin complex to tropomyosin, a structural rather than calcium-sensing role.
Correct — troponin C is the calcium-binding subunit that triggers the conformational change.
Tropomyosin physically blocks the myosin-binding site and moves in response to the troponin complex, but does not bind calcium directly.
exp: Calcium released from the SR binds troponin C, causing a conformational change transmitted through troponin I and troponin T that shifts tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin, allowing cross-bridge cycling and contraction to proceed — the core molecular sequence of excitation-contraction coupling.

subject: Physiology
q: The central chemoreceptors located near the ventral surface of the medulla primarily respond to changes in which parameter to regulate ventilation?
opts: Cerebrospinal fluid H+ concentration, driven by CO2 diffusing across the blood-brain barrier
why: Direct PaO2 sensing is a peripheral (carotid/aortic body) chemoreceptor function, not central.
Correct — central chemoreceptors respond to CSF H+, which reflects arterial CO2 diffusing across the blood-brain barrier.
Oxygen saturation sensing is also a peripheral chemoreceptor function via the carotid bodies.
Carotid bodies are chemoreceptors, not baroreceptors; arterial stretch is sensed separately by baroreceptors in the carotid sinus.
exp: CO2 diffuses freely across the blood-brain barrier into the CSF, where it hydrates to form carbonic acid and releases H+; central chemoreceptors sense this local CSF H+ rise (since CSF has poor buffering capacity) and drive most of the moment-to-moment ventilatory response to hypercapnia, unlike peripheral chemoreceptors, which respond mainly to hypoxia.

subject: Physiology
q: Progressive cervical dilation during labour triggers oxytocin release, which strengthens uterine contractions and further dilates the cervix. This escalating cycle is a classic example of which physiological control mechanism?
opts: Oxytocin release during labour, amplifying uterine contractions
Thermoregulatory sweating in response to heat
why: Oxytocin-uterine stretch loop escalates rather than corrects, the defining feature of positive feedback
Baroreceptor reflex is negative feedback correcting BP deviations
Sweating is negative feedback restoring core temperature
Insulin-glucose is negative feedback restoring euglycemia
exp: Positive feedback amplifies the original stimulus rather than reversing it. Cervical stretch during labour triggers oxytocin release, which increases contractions and further cervical stretch, escalating until delivery — most physiological control systems are negative feedback loops that restore a set point.

subject: Physiology
q: Which neurotransmitter is synthesized from the amino acid tryptophan?
why: Tryptophan → 5-HTP → serotonin, the correct pathway
Dopamine is synthesized from tyrosine via tyrosine hydroxylase, not tryptophan
GABA is synthesized from glutamate via glutamic acid decarboxylase
Acetylcholine is synthesized from choline and acetyl-CoA via choline acetyltransferase
exp: Serotonin (5-HT) is synthesized from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase and decarboxylation, with tryptophan hydroxylase as the rate-limiting step — this is why dietary tryptophan availability can influence serotonin synthesis.

subject: Physiology
q: The first heart sound (S1) coincides with which of the following events in the cardiac cycle?
opts: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Opening of the mitral and tricuspid valves
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
why: This describes S2, not S1
Valve opening does not generate an audible heart sound in health
Correct — AV valve closure at the start of isovolumetric contraction produces S1
This describes the timing of a pathological S3, not S1
exp: S1 marks the onset of ventricular systole and is produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid (AV) valves as ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure; S2 corresponds to semilunar valve closure, and an audible S3 during rapid filling is pathological in most adults.

subject: Physiology
q: Which of the following best defines anatomical dead space?
opts: The volume of alveolar air that is ventilated but not perfused by pulmonary capillary blood
The volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal tidal expiration
The volume of air remaining in the lungs after a maximal forced expiration
The volume of the conducting airways that does not participate in gas exchange (approximately 150 mL in an adult)
why: This describes alveolar dead space, one component of physiological (not anatomical) dead space
This describes expiratory reserve volume
This describes residual volume, not measurable by spirometry
Correct — conducting airway volume not participating in gas exchange
exp: Anatomical dead space is the volume of the conducting airways (nose to terminal bronchioles) where no gas exchange occurs, roughly 150 mL (~2 mL/kg) in an adult; physiological dead space adds alveolar dead space to this figure.

subject: Physiology
q: During a laboratory experiment, an isolated skeletal muscle is stimulated repeatedly with identical submaximal stimuli at a fixed short interval. Despite unchanged stimulus strength, the muscle shows progressively increasing force of contraction over the first few contractions before plateauing. Which physiological phenomenon best explains this observation?
why: Summation involves overlapping mechanical responses from rapidly repeated stimuli, not a progressive rise in twitch force at fixed submaximal strength
Tetanus is sustained fused contraction from very high stimulus frequency, not a gradual staircase rise
Correct — progressive Ca2+ accumulation with each identical stimulus
Fatigue causes progressively decreasing, not increasing, force
exp: Treppe (the staircase phenomenon) occurs when repeated stimuli of the same strength and frequency progressively increase intracellular Ca2+ availability to the contractile machinery, causing each successive twitch to strengthen until a steady state is reached — distinct from summation and tetanus.

subject: Physiology
q: A 60 kg man with acute blood loss is given 3 litres of intravenous isotonic (0.9%) saline as resuscitation fluid. Assuming no ongoing losses, in which body fluid compartment will the majority of this infused fluid ultimately distribute?
opts: Equally between intracellular and extracellular fluid
why: Correct — isotonic fluid without free water stays in the ECF compartment
Intracellular distribution requires a hypotonic (free-water) fluid, not isotonic saline
This pattern applies to hypotonic fluids like D5W after glucose metabolism, not isotonic saline
Ignores the larger interstitial redistribution that occurs with crystalloid
exp: Isotonic saline has the same effective osmolality as plasma, so it creates no osmotic gradient across cell membranes and stays confined to the ECF, distributing roughly 25% intravascular and 75% interstitial — this is why 3-4 times the estimated blood loss volume of crystalloid is needed for resuscitation.

subject: Physiology
q: A 26-year-old woman with a missed period presents with acute abdominal pain and new-onset pain at the tip of her right shoulder. Ultrasound reveals free fluid in the pelvis, consistent with a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Which physiological mechanism best explains the shoulder-tip pain in this presentation?
opts: Direct compression of the brachial plexus by intra-abdominal fluid
Referred pain from convergence of diaphragmatic (phrenic, C3-C5) and cutaneous shoulder afferents on the same spinal cord segments
Reflex spasm of the trapezius muscle secondary to hypovolemia
Direct irritation of the shoulder joint capsule by peritoneal fluid
why: The brachial plexus is anatomically unrelated to intraperitoneal fluid collections
Correct — shared spinal segment convergence between phrenic and shoulder cutaneous afferents
Hypovolemia does not cause reflex trapezius spasm
Peritoneal fluid does not physically contact the shoulder joint
exp: Hemoperitoneum irritates the undersurface of the diaphragm, whose sensory supply travels via the phrenic nerve (C3-C5); these afferents converge with cutaneous afferents from the shoulder dermatome at the same spinal cord segments, so pain is perceived at the shoulder tip — a classic example of visceral referred pain.

subject: Physiology
q: A 45-year-old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis undergoes pulmonary function testing. Both his FEV1 and FVC are found to be reduced proportionately. Which of the following best describes the expected pattern?
opts: FEV1/FVC ratio normal or increased, restrictive pattern
FEV1/FVC ratio normal, with both FEV1 and FVC also normal
FEV1/FVC ratio reduced, with increased total lung capacity
why: Correct — proportionate reduction in both volumes with preserved or raised ratio defines a restrictive pattern
Describes obstructive disease, not fibrosis
Contradicts the stem, which states both values are reduced
Restrictive disease reduces, not increases, total lung capacity
exp: In restrictive lung disease such as pulmonary fibrosis, both FEV1 and FVC decrease proportionately (FVC often falls slightly more), so the FEV1/FVC ratio remains normal or even rises — the opposite pattern to obstructive disease, where the ratio falls because airflow, not lung volume, is primarily impaired.

subject: Physiology
q: In an experimental model, reduced NaCl delivery to the macula densa of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (as occurs with a fall in GFR) triggers a compensatory response. What is the net physiological effect of this tubuloglomerular feedback mechanism?
opts: Increased renin release and afferent arteriolar dilation, restoring GFR toward normal
Decreased renin release and afferent arteriolar constriction, further reducing GFR
Direct constriction of the efferent arteriole only, independent of renin
Increased ADH secretion from the posterior pituitary
why: Correct — this is the compensatory direction of tubuloglomerular feedback
This is the opposite of the actual response and would worsen the fall in GFR
The response is not efferent-arteriole-selective and is renin-mediated
ADH secretion is governed by osmoreceptors and baroreceptors, not by macula densa NaCl sensing
exp: Low NaCl delivery to the macula densa signals reduced GFR; the juxtaglomerular apparatus responds by increasing renin release and dilating the afferent arteriole, both acting to raise glomerular capillary pressure and restore GFR — a key intrinsic renal autoregulatory mechanism distinct from the myogenic mechanism.

subject: Physiology
q: An elite 100-metre sprinter's leg muscles generate very high forces rapidly but fatigue quickly, relying predominantly on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP production. Which skeletal muscle fiber type predominates in these muscles?
why: Type I fibers are used for endurance, not explosive sprinting
Type IIa fibers are intermediate, using both oxidative and glycolytic metabolism, but are not the dominant fiber for pure sprint power
Correct — fast glycolytic fibers dominate explosive, fatiguable activity
Skeletal muscle does not contain cardiac-type fibers
exp: Type IIb (fast glycolytic) fibers have high myosin ATPase activity, few mitochondria, and rely primarily on anaerobic glycolysis, producing rapid, powerful, but short-lived contractions ideally suited to sprinting — contrasting with Type I fibers, which are used for sustained endurance activity.

subject: Physiology
q: A soldier deployed in extreme desert heat loses approximately 4 litres of hypotonic sweat over the course of a day, with inadequate water replacement. What is the expected effect on his plasma osmolality and ADH (vasopressin) secretion?
opts: Decreased plasma osmolality, decreased ADH secretion
Increased plasma osmolality, decreased ADH secretion
No change in plasma osmolality, decreased ADH secretion
Increased plasma osmolality, increased ADH secretion and thirst
why: The direction of the osmolality change is wrong — hypotonic fluid loss raises, not lowers, osmolality
Osmolality direction is correct but ADH should rise, not fall, in response
Hypotonic fluid loss without replacement does change plasma osmolality
Correct — hypotonic loss concentrates plasma, driving both ADH release and thirst
exp: Sweat is hypotonic relative to plasma, so its loss without adequate water replacement concentrates the remaining body fluid, raising plasma osmolality; hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect this rise and stimulate both ADH release and the thirst mechanism to restore osmolality toward normal.

subject: Physiology
q: Renshaw cells in the spinal cord ventral horn mediate which type of inhibition of the alpha motor neuron that activated them?
why: Correct — Renshaw cell inhibition is a feedback loop onto the same motor neuron that excited it, hence "recurrent".
Reciprocal inhibition (via Ia inhibitory interneurons) inhibits the antagonist muscle's motor neuron, a different circuit.
Presynaptic inhibition acts on the afferent terminal before the synapse, not via a feedback loop from the motor neuron itself.
Autogenic inhibition is mediated by Golgi tendon organs via Ib afferents, not by Renshaw cells.
exp: Renshaw cells are inhibitory interneurons in the ventral horn receiving a collateral from the alpha motor neuron axon, feeding glycinergic inhibition back onto that same motor neuron (and synergists) — this negative feedback loop limits excessive motor neuron firing.

subject: Physiology
q: Stretch of the right atrial wall by increased venous return causes a reflex increase in heart rate. What is this reflex called?
why: The baroreceptor reflex (carotid sinus/aortic arch) responds to arterial pressure changes and typically causes bradycardia with rising pressure, the opposite direction.
The Bezold-Jarisch reflex is a cardioinhibitory reflex from ventricular mechanoreceptors, causing bradycardia and hypotension.
Chemoreceptor reflexes respond to hypoxia/hypercapnia at the carotid/aortic bodies, not atrial stretch.
Correct — atrial stretch causing reflex tachycardia is the Bainbridge reflex.
exp: The Bainbridge reflex is triggered by stretch receptors in the right atrial wall and great vein junctions sensing increased venous return, producing reflex tachycardia via vagal afferents/sympathetic efferents — it helps prevent damming of blood in the venous and pulmonary circulation.

subject: Physiology
q: Renal blood flow remains relatively constant despite fluctuations in mean arterial pressure between approximately what range, due to autoregulation?
why: This range is too low and does not reflect the physiologic autoregulatory plateau.
Correct — 80–180 mmHg is the classic teaching range for renal autoregulation.
This range extends too high for the described autoregulatory plateau.
This range is far below normal physiologic pressures and does not match autoregulation limits.
exp: Renal autoregulation (myogenic mechanism and tubuloglomerular feedback) keeps renal blood flow/GFR relatively constant across a mean arterial pressure range of roughly 80–180 mmHg; below this range, renal blood flow becomes pressure-dependent, explaining pre-renal azotemia with hypotension.

subject: Physiology
q: A rightward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve caused by increased PCO2, decreased pH, and increased temperature — favoring oxygen unloading at the tissues — is known as what?
why: The Haldane effect describes how oxygenation of hemoglobin promotes CO2 release — about CO2 carriage, not O2 affinity shift.
The Root effect is a fish-specific phenomenon affecting hemoglobin oxygen-carrying capacity, not relevant to mammalian physiology.
Correct — the Bohr effect is the CO2/pH/temperature-driven rightward shift of the O2-Hb curve.
This is loosely associated with the Haldane effect, not the Bohr effect.
exp: The Bohr effect: increased CO2, decreased pH (increased H+), and increased temperature decrease hemoglobin's O2 affinity, shifting the dissociation curve right — advantageous at metabolizing tissues where CO2/acid production is high and O2 unloading is needed.

subject: Physiology
q: A 68-year-old man is found to have a 6 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm on ultrasound screening. His vascular surgeon explains that as the aneurysm enlarges, the risk of rupture rises disproportionately because wall tension increases with radius even at the same blood pressure. Which physiological principle explains this?
why: Correct — the Law of Laplace directly relates wall tension to radius at constant pressure, explaining rupture risk with growing aneurysm size.
The Frank-Starling law relates ventricular preload (stretch) to stroke volume, not vessel wall tension.
Poiseuille's law governs flow through a tube as a function of radius, pressure gradient, viscosity, and length, not wall tension.
Fick's principle is used to calculate cardiac output from oxygen consumption and arteriovenous oxygen difference, unrelated to wall tension.
exp: The Law of Laplace states wall tension is proportional to pressure times radius, so as an aneurysm's radius increases at constant intraluminal pressure, wall tension rises proportionally — explaining why larger aneurysms are disproportionately prone to rupture (basis of surgical size thresholds, generally ≥5.5cm in men).

subject: Physiology
q: A 35-year-old man sustains a stab injury causing right-sided hemisection of the spinal cord at T10. On examination, he has ipsilateral loss of motor power and vibration/proprioception below the lesion, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation starting a couple of segments below the lesion. What is this syndrome called?
why: Anterior cord syndrome causes bilateral loss of motor function and pain/temperature with preserved dorsal column sensation, not the asymmetric picture described.
Central cord syndrome classically causes disproportionate upper-limb weakness (often after hyperextension injury in the elderly), not this crossed sensory-motor pattern.
Posterior cord syndrome selectively affects dorsal columns bilaterally, not a hemisection pattern.
Correct — the ipsilateral motor/dorsal column loss with contralateral pain/temperature loss is the classic Brown-Séquard pattern from cord hemisection.
exp: Brown-Séquard syndrome results from spinal cord hemisection: ipsilateral loss of motor function (corticospinal) and vibration/proprioception (dorsal columns, uncrossed at that level), with contralateral loss of pain/temperature (spinothalamic, which decussates within 1-2 segments of entry).

subject: Physiology
q: A 75-year-old man reports dizziness and near-syncope on standing up quickly from bed. His blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg supine, falling to 100/65 mmHg with a rise in heart rate from 72 to 90/min within 1 minute of standing. Which physiological mechanism normally limits this fall in blood pressure on standing, and appears blunted here?
why: Renal autoregulation maintains renal blood flow/GFR, not the immediate beat-to-beat BP response to postural change.
Correct — the baroreceptor reflex is the primary rapid-response mechanism buffering BP change on standing.
The Bainbridge reflex responds to atrial stretch/increased venous return, the opposite scenario to reduced venous return on standing.
The Bohr effect concerns oxygen-hemoglobin affinity, unrelated to blood pressure regulation.
exp: On standing, gravitational pooling reduces venous return/BP; carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors sense this and rapidly trigger reflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction via reduced vagal/increased sympathetic outflow. Blunting of this reflex (age-related or autonomic dysfunction) causes orthostatic hypotension.

subject: Physiology
q: A mountaineer ascends rapidly to 4500 m altitude and within hours develops increased respiratory rate and depth, despite a falling arterial PCO2. Which receptors are primarily responsible for this early hyperventilatory response to hypoxia?
opts: J receptors in the alveolar walls
Stretch receptors in the bronchial smooth muscle
why: Central chemoreceptors respond to CSF H+/PCO2, and falling PCO2 at altitude would reduce their drive, not increase it, so they are not the primary driver here.
J receptors respond to pulmonary interstitial congestion, producing rapid shallow breathing in conditions like pulmonary edema, not hypoxic drive.
Correct — only peripheral chemoreceptors sense hypoxia directly and drive the hyperventilatory response at altitude.
Bronchial stretch receptors mediate the Hering-Breuer reflex limiting over-inflation, unrelated to hypoxic drive.
exp: Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) are the only receptors responding directly to falling arterial PO2, driving hyperventilation at high altitude even as falling PCO2 would otherwise suppress central chemoreceptor drive — this hypoxic ventilatory response is the initial acclimatization mechanism before renal compensation for the resulting respiratory alkalosis.

subject: Physiology
q: A 40-year-old woman presents with fluctuating ptosis and diplopia that worsen through the day and with sustained upward gaze. Repetitive nerve stimulation at low frequency shows a progressive decrement in compound muscle action potential amplitude. What is the underlying neuromuscular defect?
opts: Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channel dysfunction (Lambert-Eaton syndrome)
Presynaptic acetylcholine vesicle release failure due to botulinum toxin
why: Correct — fatigable ptosis/diplopia with a decremental RNS response is the classic picture of myasthenia gravis.
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome shows the opposite pattern — an incremental response on high-frequency stimulation, and strength improves briefly with exercise, not the decrement described here.
Failure of acetylcholinesterase (e.g., organophosphate poisoning) causes prolonged depolarization and a cholinergic crisis, not fatigable fluctuating weakness with decrement.
Botulinum toxin causes descending flaccid paralysis with autonomic features from irreversible presynaptic release blockade, not the fluctuating, fatigable pattern here.
exp: Myasthenia gravis is caused by autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors at the NMJ, producing fatigable weakness and a characteristic decremental response on low-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation, since fewer receptors are available as vesicular ACh stores deplete with repeated firing.

subject: Physiology
q: A 3-year-old child with acute bacterial tonsillitis develops fever of 39.5°C with shivering and cold extremities, despite the ambient temperature being warm. Her mother notices the child feels cold and shivers even though her core temperature is rising. What best explains this shivering phase?
opts: The hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point has been raised by pyrogens, and the body is generating heat to reach the new set point
The child has developed hypothermia due to sepsis
Peripheral vasodilation is causing excess heat loss
why: Correct — a raised hypothalamic set point drives shivering and vasoconstriction until core temperature "catches up," the physiological chill phase of fever.
This is a febrile response with a raised set point, not true hypothermia, which would mean an abnormally low set point or failure of thermoregulation.
Peripheral vasoconstriction (not vasodilation) occurs during the chill phase to conserve heat and raise core temperature toward the new set point.
Sweating is suppressed, not failed, during the rising phase of fever, as the body is trying to conserve/generate heat, not lose it.
exp: Endogenous pyrogens (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha) act on the hypothalamus via PGE2 to raise the thermoregulatory set point; until core temperature reaches the new higher set point, the body perceives itself as too cold, triggering shivering and vasoconstriction — the chill/rigor phase preceding the fever plateau.

subject: Physiology
q: A 55-year-old man presents with an unsteady, wide-based gait, intention tremor that worsens as his hand approaches a target, dysdiadochokinesia, and slurred, scanning speech following a posterior fossa stroke. Which structure is most likely involved?
why: Basal ganglia lesions typically produce resting tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia (as in Parkinsonism), not intention tremor or dysdiadochokinesia.
Correct — this constellation of ataxia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, and scanning speech localizes to the cerebellum.
Anterior spinal cord lesions cause bilateral motor and pain/temperature loss below the lesion, not cerebellar-type incoordination.
Dorsal column lesions cause loss of proprioception/vibration with sensory ataxia (worse with eyes closed, Romberg positive), not intention tremor or dysarthria.
exp: Cerebellar lesions produce ipsilateral ataxia — wide-based gait, dysmetria/intention tremor (worsening near the target, unlike basal ganglia resting tremor), dysdiadochokinesia, and scanning dysarthria — because the cerebellum coordinates timing/amplitude of voluntary movement rather than initiating it.

subject: Physiology
q: Which of the following is a classic example of primary active transport across a cell membrane?
opts: Facilitated diffusion of glucose via GLUT transporters
why: Correct - Na+-K+ ATPase directly hydrolyses ATP to pump ions against their gradient
SGLT1 is secondary active transport using the Na+ gradient, not direct ATP hydrolysis
Na+-H+ exchanger is also secondary active (antiport) transport
GLUT-mediated glucose uptake is passive facilitated diffusion needing no energy input
